#328. California fights "preposterous" Trump admin demand to scrap state broadband laws

State tries to obtain broadband funds despite rejecting Trump admin condition.

California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration’s demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations.

California’s stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds.

The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided last year that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction. California is slated to spend $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations and may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion from BEAD for a mix of deployment and non-deployment projects.

State officials argue that California should be able to obtain the money and keep enforcing its laws, because the Trump administration’s demand would violate the state’s constitutional rights. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) made its view clear in a carefully worded letter yesterday to Assistant Secretary of Commerce and NTIA Administrator Arielle Roth.

“The CPUC cannot be bound by any terms or conditions that are unconstitutional or not authorized by law and it expressly does not waive or concede any arguments or challenges concerning the legality, interpretation, or applicability of any term or condition,” CPUC President John Reynolds told Roth.

Reynolds’ letter also said the CPUC cannot prevent other California agencies from enforcing state laws, suggesting that the attorney general would maintain the right to punish misbehaving Internet providers.

Reynolds’ letter acknowledged that the NTIA may not agree with the CPUC’s stance and said the state thus will not distribute any funding to ISPs until after the state and federal agency sort out any differences. If the NTIA refuses to change its position, California could sue the Trump administration on the grounds that the condition is unconstitutional.

The NTIA does not appear likely to bend. “As noted in the Department’s response to CPUC, the terms and conditions of the award constitute the entire agreement between NTIA and CPUC. No part of the letter outlining CPUC’s concerns is incorporated into or made part of the award,” an NTIA spokesperson told Ars today.

Consumer advocacy group Public Knowledge supported CPUC’s position. The Trump administration’s demand to preempt state laws is “brazen and meritless,” the group said.

The CPUC voted to ratify the funding plan in September. But Reynolds said in yesterday’s letter to the Trump administration that his agency’s acceptance of the funds is “based on the CPUC’s best understanding of the effect of Section 50” of the BEAD terms and conditions. Section 50 of the BEAD rules says each state:

shall commit that it will not enforce any law, regulation, order, contracting requirement, or other enforceable obligation that directly or indirectly regulates the rates, terms, and conditions of broadband Internet service… or imposes net neutrality rules, open access, or other utility-style rules on broadband Internet service, against a Subgrantee or its affiliates anywhere it provides service within the State (i.e., both BEAD and non-BEAD locations), while that Subgrantee has any subgrant that is still within its period of performance, extended period of performance, or federal interest period.

The BEAD rules specify that a net neutrality rule is one prohibiting ISPs from “blocking content, throttling speeds, imposing data caps, or engaging in paid prioritization.” ISPs obtaining BEAD funding could be exempt from such laws for up to 14 years.

Reynolds’ letter said the NTIA-imposed condition is “vague and ambiguous as to its scope and its relationship to Section 47 U.S.C. § 1702(g)(2)(A)(i) of the BEAD statute,” the US law that created the BEAD program. He wrote:

The CPUC does not interpret Section 50 to require the CPUC to waive, release, or otherwise forfeit any rights, claims, arguments, or defenses concerning potential implications of Section 50 that may violate applicable laws. Further, the CPUC’s acceptance of funds under this award should not be understood as agreement either to refrain from compliance with mandatory legal duties or obligations, or to constrain other State of California entities in the exercise of their authorities to enforce state law, which is outside the scope of the CPUC’s authority. Moreover, California’s net neutrality law expressly provides that “any waiver of the provisions of this title is contrary to public policy and shall be unenforceable and void.” Likewise, many of the CPUC’s own programs that touch on broadband Internet access service are mandated by the California Public Utilities Code, and are neither discretionary nor waivable.

The NTIA today updated its BEAD progress dashboard to reflect that California has signed its final agreement with the federal agency. California was the last state or territory to turn in its final agreement.

“All 56 states and territories have signed and returned their award agreement, finalizing the process,” the NTIA’s updated dashboard page said.

California could face legal problems if and when it distributes the money, which is to be given to Internet service providers in exchange for deploying broadband in unserved and underserved areas. ISPs could insist that they don’t have to follow state law and sue California or simply decide to violate consumer protection laws and defend against any lawsuits the state attorney general might file against them.

Reynolds apparently hopes to avoid that outcome by holding discussions with the NTIA to resolve any disagreement over the enforceability of California state law.

“To the extent that NTIA and the CPUC disagree about the CPUC’s obligations under Section 50 and other terms and conditions, the CPUC will execute any subgrant agreements if and when the CPUC and NTIA are able to resolve such disagreements and any other applicable conditions are met,” Reynolds wrote. “To that end, we will direct our staff to work diligently and cooperatively with NTIA staff to find such a solution.”

Whether California’s strategy works “depends on what happens next,” Stanford Law professor Barbara van Schewick, a longtime proponent of net neutrality and other telecom regulations, told Ars today.

“The letter doesn’t change the terms of California’s award: Condition 50 is still in it, and only a court or NTIA agreeing in writing can take it out,” she said. “The letter puts California’s position on the record before any contracts with providers are signed and preserves California’s legal arguments against Condition 50.”

Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office declined to comment when contacted by Ars today. A spokesperson for California Gov. Gavin Newsom said California is not giving up its right to enforce state laws against Internet providers.

“California is accepting federal broadband funding to bring high-speed Internet to hundreds of thousands of homes and businesses, many of them in rural and underserved communities,” a governor’s spokesperson said in a statement provided to Ars. “We’re ready to get these projects built with our local and federal partners. Connecting these communities is the goal, and so is protecting them. California’s laws, including our net neutrality protections, still stand.”

California’s net neutrality law prohibits ISPs from blocking or throttling lawful traffic and says ISPs may not require fees from websites or online services to deliver or prioritize their traffic to Internet users. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws, and California defeated ISPs that challenged the state law in court.

California also has a law that prohibits mobile providers from throttling first responders during emergencies. That law was passed in 2019, a year after Verizon throttled an “unlimited” data plan used by Santa Clara County firefighters during a wildfire. Local wildfire-preparedness groups warned that the BEAD condition could prevent California from enforcing the throttling law and requirements for battery backups on cell towers.

According to van Schewick, “California has strong arguments that Condition 50 is illegal. Congress designed BEAD to get broadband built while making sure the providers who take the money follow the law: the statute directs states to ensure funded providers can carry out their work ‘in compliance with all applicable Federal, State, and local laws.’”

But van Schewick said the letter is just an initial step. “The real test comes the first time a BEAD provider blocks a competitor’s app, throttles firefighters, or walks away from a price commitment,” she said. “If the state enforces its laws when that happens, the letter will have protected Californians. If the state looks the other way, Condition 50 will have worked exactly as the providers intended, without a single court ever ruling on it.”

#327. Chelsea searches for new manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s plan for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected new signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

#323. BMW reports lower Q3 earnings as China woes mount

BMW reports a drop in profits in the July to September quarter amid fierce competition from China.

German carmaker BMW reported a nearly 15% drop in third-quarter net profit on Wednesday, as competition from China shakes the global car industry.

Net profit for the third quarter fell to 1.45 billion euros ($1.61 billion), while sales fell nearly 6% to 30.45 billion euros, BMW said.

The main cause of the decline was BMW's poor business in China. Although the company sold more cars in the US and Europe compared to the same period last year, this could only partially offset the decline in China.

BMW's car deliveries in China, which were already at their lowest level since 2017 last year, fell 24.8% in the quarter and consequently dragged global deliveries down by 6.3.

CEO Milan Nedeljkovic said his company would "specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

BMW on Tuesday also lowered its outlook for the current year, citing the faster-than-planned implementation of restructuring measures that includes 8,000 layoffs in its home market.

German carmakers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market,  resulting in cost-cutting measures.

Volkswagen, the world's second-largest carmaker, is battling mounting competition from falling demand in its core Chinese market.

BMW, and its industry heavyweight peers, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Volkswagen Group posted its worst quarterly results in more than a decade earlier this October.

It is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW has announced that it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.

On the other hand, German auto parts supplier Schaeffler announced on Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe, by 2028.

According to the company statement, three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany.

German automotive supplier Bosch, the world's biggest, announced last year that it would cut 13,000 jobs, mostly in its auto division.

#322. The DEA banned a drug some opioid users called a miracle

Researchers say the Schedule I ban could kill studies of a promising opioid treatment.

In 2012, as the driver of deaths in the opioid crisis began moving from prescription pills to heroin, Laura Bohn was tasked with finding safer drugs to manage pain.

Funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, in 2017 she and other scientists revealed in the science journal Cell that several compounds—including a particularly promising one called SR-17018—could relieve pain in mice without causing respiratory depression. That’s a big deal, because respiratory depression is typically what causes people using opioids to stop breathing and die.

Bohn, senior associate vice president of research at University of South Florida Health, says her team filed a patent on SR-17018. They went on to discover that mice using the chemical did not develop a high tolerance for it and that mice already dependent on morphine—a powerful opioid—could consume SR-17018 to reset their tolerance without suffering from painful withdrawal symptoms.

It’s no longer just mice who use SR-17018.

On Reddit and Discord, people who use drugs frequently refer to the compound as a godsend that’s helped them quit using opioids they’re addicted to. Until very recently, the drug, though not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration, was relatively easy to purchase online, as it was not a federally controlled substance. Bohn, meanwhile, has been in the process of trying to conduct clinical trials on humans, which has never been done.

But all of that came crashing to a halt when the US Drug Enforcement Administration emergency-scheduled SR-17018 as a Schedule I controlled substance in late August, putting it in the same category as heroin with “no currently accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse.”

For Bohn, the move will make it much harder to do the research she’s been planning. “It’s a real hassle,” she tells WIRED. “Right now, I would like to have it tested for additional safety studies, and I can’t have it made, I can’t ship it, I can’t touch it. I can’t do anything.”

For drug users who hope to use it to wean off opioids—despite the lack of clinical evidence that the drug is effective in humans—it’s the removal of a potential off-ramp for their addictions.

Jim Bates has been hooked on various opioids, including prescription pills, heroin, and fentanyl, since he was 25. About two years ago, the 53-year-old Duncan, Oklahoma, kitchen manager got addicted to 7-OH, a concentrated compound found in kratom that activates the brain’s opioid receptors. “That shit blew my head off,” he says, noting he was introduced to it at a vape shop. “It was a whole lot like heroin.”

He eventually graduated to a similar chemical, called MGM-15, which felt more like oxycodone—the effect he prefers. (The DEA placed both 7-OH and MGM-15 in Schedule I over the summer.)

It got to the point where MGM-15 was “all I was thinking about,” Bates says. About 11 months ago, he started scouring the Discord and Telegram groups he was in for advice on how to quit.

“I got introduced to SR-17, which was a freaking miracle,” he says, using a common shorthand for the chemical. It took him about three weeks to taper off MGM-15, using SR-17018.

Previous attempts to get off 7-OH had caused him “anxiety like you wouldn’t believe” along with restless legs during withdrawal, he says. But with SR-17018, he didn’t experience any physical withdrawal symptoms. “They’ve never created anything like this,” he says, adding that he didn’t experience a high or “euphoria” from taking it.

While he says SR-17018 didn’t take away every negative side effect of coming off opioids, “the anxiety and the sweating and the restlessness and all that stuff was gone.” He says he was able to keep working, with “no huge disruption in my life.”

Both men have used gold-standard drugs for getting off opioids—buprenorphine and methadone—but say they prefer SR-17018 because it doesn’t have to be used long-term. Getting off buprenorphine and methadone can also cause intense withdrawal symptoms.

Michael speculates that the feds may have banned SR-17018 because they saw it as a “potential disruptor to a multibillion-dollar industry.” “I think that that’s why they’re freaked out about SR becoming widely known and available, because it is going to help a lot of people get off of these maintenance drugs that they’re stuck on.”

When Denver attorney Robert Rush caught wind that the DEA was planning to emergency schedule SR-17018, he filed a request to stop it, arguing that it has a lower risk profile than the other synthetic opioids being banned at the time. He tells me the DEA never responded.

“It was a very reasonable, well-thought-out, grounded-in-scientific-evidence argument, and they just completely ignored it,” says Rush, who is executive director of the nonprofit Rights and Reason Project—which advocates for drug policy reform—and represents Bohn.

In response to a request for comment, the DEA referred WIRED to its notice of intent to schedule SR-17018 and three other synthetic opioids. The document says the agency had found two samples of the drug in two states since 2025 via the National Forensic Laboratory Information System, which analyzes samples of drugs seized by law enforcement. It also said a separate drug monitoring system, Rapid Drug Analysis and Research, had detected some samples of SR-17018 on the West Coast.

“The four synthetic opioids have no currently approved medical use and, based on positive identifications of these four substances in forensic drug exhibits and toxicology samples, are likely to be trafficked and abused similarly to other synthetic opioids,” the notice of intent says. It also says that because SR-17018 can reset a person’s opioid tolerance, it might leave them more vulnerable to overdose the next time they use—though the same is true for abstinence.

Rush says the DEA’s use of temporary emergency scheduling powers in this case is “draconian” and shouldn’t apply, because SR-17018 hasn’t been implicated in emergency room visits or overdose deaths.

The emergency scheduling will last two years, with a potential one-year extension—but the DEA could also permanently schedule the drug in that time period, a process that requires public and scientific input. During the emergency scheduling period, Rush says, there’s no opportunity for a judge to review the DEA’s decision.

He says that the DEA banning gas station opioids like 7-OH while simultaneously getting rid of potentially helpful substances like SR-17018 “is setting up a perfect storm for another overdose crisis.”

“I cannot find a compelling reason to shut down a couple of decades’ worth of research into something that could either be or lead to the development of next-generation opioid dependency treatment,” he says.

Even after all my testing, if someone asks for the quickest, no-fuss way to find a hookup, my answer is still Tinder. CEO Spencer Rascoff is actively trying to move the app away from its "hookup reputation" to attract Gen Z and bring in more women, but there's likely only one reason you're here.

The irony? His strategy is helping horny singles get laid. New user registrations returned to year-over-year growth in March 2026, per Match Group's latest financials, and daily active users were down just 1 percent in August, Tinder's best showing in years. With over 100 billion connections made worldwide, hookups aren't hard to come by. (Pro tip: Use the "Free Tonight" feature, especially on weekends.)

It's built for rapid-fire connections, not lengthy love stories (though some people, including Mashable's Tech Editor, met their long-term partner on the app).

"Tinder, hands down, is the best app for hookups," Michelle Herzog, LMFT and AASECT-certified sex therapist, tells Mashable. "Over the past decade or so, it’s morphed from being the early 20s hookup central to a place for adults of all ages to go for a quick one-nighter." Weiss adds that it's "probably the most popular hookup app among college students."

Even when Tinder plays dress-up as a serious relationship platform (see: turning "Double Date" into "Modes" and launching the reality show Double Date Island), it's still the undisputed heavyweight champion of casual flings. You can use "Double Date" for low-pressure group hangouts, and Tinder's "Year in Swipe" data crowned 2026 the year of "Clear-Coding," aka laying your intentions on the table so nobody wastes their time.

The newest way to take the pressure off? Group Hangouts, which launched Sept. 30. You and at least two friends pick an activity and "like" other groups. Tinder plans to expand "Events" to 75 cities by the end of 2026, and about 30 percent of events are free. Scammers found workarounds, but Match Group says Face Check and its other safety updates have cut exposure to potential bad actors by more than 60 percent, and it invests $125 million a year in trust and safety. The change came straight from user feedback: a Bumble survey found that 66 percent of women actually prefer men to send the first message.

Men, this is your moment, so don't waste it on "hey girl." "Read her profile and talk to her like a human being," says Arrechea. "Not 'hey.' Not a copy-and-pasted pickup line." Even on a hookup-friendly app, lead with something from her profile, not your best pickup line.

This update fully replaces Bumble's previous "Opening Moves" feature. And about those rumors that Bumble's AI assistant, "Bee," would replace swiping? CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd shut that down on the company's latest earnings call: "Let me be clear: Bee is not replacing the swipe. We are not aiming for an AI-driven experience. Bee is simply the intelligence under the hood," she said. She's keeping whatever does replace the swipe under wraps for now, with bigger profile and IRL updates expected in early 2027. In the meantime, Bumble added profile badges for "ethical non-monogamy" and "intimacy without commitment," making it easier to flag exactly what you want.

Once your profile is set, Bumble is testing new ways to help you meet up IRL. They're currently testing a "Suggest a Date" feature in Canada to bypass the tedious back-and-forth. (And don't worry about losing your agency; in Canadian tests of these recent changes, 92 percent of women said they still felt in control of their dating experience.)

If you're burned out on one-on-one setups, the app is also launching a standalone event-curation app called "Plans" to help singles meet up in curated small groups in person. You can also use the "Instant Match" QR code to vet your real-life crushes at a bar and check their verified status before you decide to go home with them.

However, it's worth being upfront about the app's fumbles. A class-action lawsuit alleges that Bumble failed to protect user data during a "massive" breach by the hacker group ShinyHunters earlier this year. Reuters reported in late June that Bumble is exploring a potential sale, and its paying user base has dropped to 3.2 million, down 24 percent from two years ago. Even Blackstone, one of its biggest investors, is cashing out.

Despite the drama and a challenging market, Bumble still offers solid functionality. You can chat via text, voice, or video without spending a dime, and free users still have access to basic filters like age, distance, and verified profiles. While premium features (Bumble Boost or premium membership) offer advanced filters, they're not essential for finding a potential hookup buddy.

Feeld is for the explorers: the singles, couples, and polycules looking to ethically explore non-monogamy, kink, and alternative relationship styles. If you find the binary options on most dating apps to be limiting, Feeld's inclusive, consent-forward environment is refreshing. It’s a hub for people practicing "relationship anarchy" or just curious about connections without traditional rules.

It's worth noting, however, that the app is attracting more "vanilla" users (those with conventional tastes) lately, which is changing the dynamic somewhat. But even those "normies" might be hiding a wild side: Feeld's "State of Reflections Volume 1: Am I Normal?" report found that 42 percent of mainstream, non-Feeld daters actually practice kink. And the community is getting more curious by the day.

"Heteroflexible" is the fastest-growing sexuality on the app, and interest in pegging among cis men has surged. It's proof that this is still the place to go if you want to explore outside the box. And yes, the nerds are here. New Feeld data found that tabletop gamers are 65 percent more likely to be non-monogamous than other users, and more than half of Gen Z Feeld members list ethical non-monogamy as an interest.

Feeld joins Hinge and Hily on the very short list of dating apps that are gaining new users, even as other apps struggle.

The free “Constellation” feature lets you be transparent by linking your profile with up to five partners, and you can use more than 20 labels to define those connections, from "Lover" and "Dom" to "Friend with benefits." (While this feature links your profiles, your private chat histories and existing connections are not shared with your partners.) The app also offers detailed desire and kink tags, from "Bondage" to "Cuddling," so you can find exactly what you're looking for.

"Feeld is a good app for finding hookups because the people on it are sexually open-minded but also conscious," says Weiss. "Many of them are looking for casual sexual encounters, but not 'casual' in the sense of wanting to make a conquest or put in minimal effort," she adds. "I often recommend this app to couples who want to find a third person to play with or date, as well as singles who want to explore different sexual fantasies and subcultures."

To make articulating those desires even easier, Feeld launched an interactive quiz called "Reflections" that helps you map out your boundaries, relationships, and kink affinities. According to Feeld's May 2026 "State of Reflections Volume 2: The Words We Didn’t Have" report, it's super effective for skipping the small talk and getting down to business. After taking the quiz, 72 percent of users said they changed (or thought about changing) how they communicate their desires on their profiles, and over half felt more empowered to bring up boundaries and safe sex right from the start. Once you finish the quiz, you get a custom link and QR code to share your dealbreakers with potential partners before you even meet.

If you're still figuring out how to put your relationship structure into words, Weiss suggests keeping it playful: "You can write something cute like 'ethical slut' or 'I have room for more than one love of my life in my heart' instead of just using the technical language."

If you're tired of Tinder, I think HUD is the best new hookup app, and its tagline is literally "Fun without strings attached." HUD stands for "Honest, Upfront, and Direct," and it's the app for people who aren’t afraid to be their most authentic selves. Translation: If you're into non-monogamy, this is where you'll find like-minded people.

The people on this app aren’t here to find their forever person, but friends with benefits is definitely on the table. You might also find kinksters, ethical non-monogamous folks, and people interested in exploring relationship styles that are a little outside the mainstream. With more than 19 million users worldwide as of 2026, HUD offers many opportunities for your next hookup.

If Hinge and Pure had a baby, it would be HUD. This app doesn’t beat around the bush, but it’s also artsy in presentation and has a kinky-fun community behind it.

Like Hinge, you can answer prompts (up to three), add photos (up to five), and note whether you’re into smoking, drinking, or drugs. There’s also a really cool "My Bedroom" feature that lets you choose three "desires" that you’re really into, three "desires" you’re "open" to, and three you’re definitely not into. Examples include "bondage," "butt stuff," and "golden showers." There are tons of "desires" to choose from, even if you’re not that kinky, so have fun with it.

Speaking of kinky, HUD just published its 2026 Pleasure Census (a global culture report in partnership with Girls Get Off). The survey revealed that 80 percent of daters aren't having as much sex as they'd ideally like, and those who openly talk about what they want in bed are three times more likely to reach orgasm with a partner every time. That's why features like "My Bedroom" are so great; they eliminate that awkward barrier to communication before you even meet up.

In addition to its "My Bedroom" feature, HUD also has an "Anti-Commitment Mode" badge you can add to your profile to let potential matches know why you're here. You’ll also get to pick your archetype (if you’re not sure what yours is, the app has a little quiz) to help you find your match. You can even add your favorite song to your profile.

Not sure how to explain that you're poly, kinky, or just not looking for anything serious? Keep it short. "You don't need to write a manifesto in your dating bio!" says Paulita Pappel, intimacy expert and founder of Lustery. "The bio is there to open the right door, not to function as a legal contract."

The chat features are also a little more developed than those in a typical hookup app. You can engage with someone’s profile just by liking or commenting on their prompts, photos, etc. The video chat option also shows both cameras blurred until you both decide to reveal yourselves. Of course, you can get more features with a premium subscription, but the free version offers a lot.

Hily (short for "Hey, I Like You") is for anyone who wants a little more substance than Tinder's fast-swipe format but doesn't want to answer a ton of questions to get set up and start matching. This new dating app gives you total flexibility: you can keep your profile simple, or fill out optional prompts, pick lifestyle passions, and take its 40-question "Icks&Clicks" compatibility quiz to see how compatible you are with potential matches before chatting.

Granted, my experience comes from living in a small Southern town (where more than 1,400 men were active at any given moment), but even compared to testing Hinge in the same spot, Hily brought out a distinct crowd. The user pool was packed with blue-collar guys, hunters, fishers, and dudes on motorcycles looking for low-pressure hangouts, casual flings, or sexting partners. While I didn't run into many queer women (mostly couples looking for a third), if you're looking for straight hookups with outdoorsy or country-leaning guys, the active user base makes finding a match easy.

Read our full review of the Hily dating app.

Even though it doesn't get as much attention as Tinder or Bumble, Hily has over 42 million users and lets you control how much effort you put into your profile. You can pick intentions like "Physical connection" or "Something casual," list up to 12 passions, and answer optional prompts under categories like "My Dating Guide" and "Life Vibes." It also features a "Roulette" wheel that hands out free daily perks like profile boosts and rollbacks.

There are a couple of quirks to keep in mind while browsing, though. While the "Finder" will show you people who match your set filters (like age, location, and gender), those preferences don't necessarily apply to who lands in your "Likes" feed. Plus, anyone who likes your profile stays blurred unless you pay for a subscription — unless you get lucky and win free "Unblurs" from the daily Roulette wheel or happen to stumble across them naturally in the "Finder."

If you're not too keen on receiving NSFW photos or chats, Hily added a feature called "Consent Guard." Built with sexologists, this tool scans incoming messages and photos for adult content and gives you a pop-up warning so you can decide whether you actually want to see a nude or explicit text before opening it. It keeps your inbox safe from surprise cyberflashing, but lets you turn up the heat as soon as you give the green light. "[Consent tools] make it less likely for users to be sexually harassed, while also allowing them to see who the culprits are so they can choose not to engage with them," says Weiss.

While other apps push AI matchmakers, Hily is taking a different approach. Their early 2026 "T.R.U.T.H. Report" showed that nearly 70 percent of daters feel AI matchmakers make dating feel fake. In response, Hily brought back its "HI" (Human Intelligence) campaign to focus on real human chemistry rather than automated matching algorithms.

Grindr is the hookup app for gay men. While there are other options on the market, Grindr is the go-to spot for most gay, bi, trans, and queer men looking for a fast connection. It's undeniably effective for finding a hookup, and the numbers prove it: Grindr's "Unwrapped" report revealed that users sent over 135 billion chats last year, with "Hung" being the most-searched profile tag.

However, as Tyler Schoeber pointed out in his review, the free tier is "overrun with intrusive ads" and limits you to viewing around 87 messageable profiles on the grid unless you pay for an upgraded subscription. Unfortunately, a Grindr XTRA membership can get pricey fast. Thankfully, Grindr's 2026 roadmap promises to improve the ad experience with "rewarded ads," which will let free users unlock premium features just by watching an ad.

The bottom line: Thanks to its wide user base, Grindr is still the go-to hookup app for gay men, even if the free version can be a pain to use.

Grindr's ability to connect you with nearby guys instantly is unmatched, especially in smaller towns where the queer community might be limited. Its location-based grid makes it incredibly easy to find someone available right now. This year, they're putting the "Right Now" feature directly onto the map so you can see exactly who's ready to hook up nearby. According to Grindr's own data (released in May), this feature is most used in places like Taiwan, the Philippines, Lima, Buenos Aires, and Medellín. They also added "Discreet Posting," which lets you post a hookup request without showing your profile until you manually approve a chat request.

Aside from getting your biscuit buttered, Grindr has become a hub for travelers. In fact, to capitalize on its global footprint, the app just dropped the third season of its Host or Travel series. This jet-setting culture led to the "Roam" feature, which lets you drop a pin anywhere in the world to scout local talent before you even pack your bags. The app's map is also getting a serious upgrade to highlight gay bars, clubs, and gyms, with direct hotel bookings currently in beta testing.

Grindr has also been flexing some serious cultural muscle, most recently teaming up with Madonna to launch her Confessions II album with a surprise Times Square concert streamed exclusively to Grindr users.

The biggest news in 2026 is that Grindr is officially entering its "AI era" — and it might cost you. The app recently started testing its ultra-premium subscription tier called "EDGE." Powered by Grindr's proprietary "gAI" stack, this tier costs $350–$500 a month and is designed to reduce scrolling. Free users aren't entirely left out, though; they'll get AI perks like real-time chat translations, a "Smart Inbox," and an AI "Wingman" to help filter matching profiles.

Last year, the company publicly supported the "App Store Accountability Act," arguing that age verification should happen at the device level (via Apple or Google) rather than forcing users to upload IDs to every app. They also added an in-app Safety Center, a "Taken on Grindr" timestamp to verify photo freshness, and rolled out impressive sexual health features (backed by their Grindr for Equality initiative), including automated HIV testing reminders, status sharing, and PrEP/DoxyPEP profile options.

There's more on the healthcare front, too. In September, Grindr agreed to acquire Freddie's parent company, PurposeMed, with plans to expand access to PrEP care through Grindr Health. The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026.

While the free experience can feel bogged down by ads that push users toward paid tiers like XTRA, Grindr is still the undisputed King for quick, location-based connections in the gay community.

HER is a platform created by and for queer women, providing a safe and inclusive space to connect with women and nonbinary folks without worrying about being sexualized by "skeevy men." Launched in 2015 to meet a growing need in the lesbian dating scene, HER isn't exclusively designed for hookups, but it offers a vibrant community where you can explore casual encounters or even find meaningful relationships. With more than 15 million users, the app is brimming with opportunity for whatever you're looking for.

HER makes it easy to signal your intentions. The "Looking for" section on your profile lets you add a "something casual" tag, which is displayed out in the open. More recently, the app introduced "Feelings," a feature that lets you add temporary, expressive tags to your profile like "Hook up" or "Flirty" to show exactly what kind of connection you're craving.

The app also functions like a social media platform, creating an inclusive space for LGBTQ+ users with a social feed, events, and media. While the interface can feel a little clunky at first, it's not too difficult to navigate. For safety, HER offers photo-verified profiles with a checkmark badge.

In 2025, HER was acquired by Match Group. The move was met with apprehension from its user base, with many on Reddit fearing the "enshittification" of another beloved queer platform. While HER founder Robyn Exton expressed optimism and Match Group CEO Spencer Rascoff pledged to "protect" what makes the app special, the sapphic community is largely holding its breath to see if they live up to that promise. Those fears aren't entirely unfounded; Match Group recently reported a 20 percent revenue increase in HER test markets due to new "monetization optimizations," which have some users wary of future paywalls.

However, the app's core features are pretty much the same. HER even kicked off the year with a new "Sapphic Restart" campaign to reassure users of its community-first approach. If you're wondering if the company still has an edge, look at its "Everything Reminds Me of HER" billboards in New York and Los Angeles. The brazen ads featured highly sensual innuendos — like champagne cascading over skin and fingers slipping into a bowling ball. The campaign went viral on TikTok and Instagram (because, why wouldn't it?), proving that at least for now, HER is keeping its unapologetic, sex-positive spirit alive. We haven't seen any major degradation in the user experience — so for now, it's still a top recommendation.

Sniffies is a web-based cruising platform built for one thing: finding sex, right now, with minimal small talk. Sniffies was deemed too hardcore for the App Store, and so it's not technically an app. It's a hookup destination for men seeking men who want spontaneous and anonymous encounters.

If you feel like Tinder and Grindr aren't direct enough, I'd like to introduce you to Sniffies, the hookup platform that brings cruising into the 21st century. It launched an official iOS app in March 2025, only to be kicked out of the App Store by May for being, well, too horny for Apple. But if you downloaded the app before it was removed, and haven't deleted it, it should still work.

As soon as you enter the website, you'll see a map of guys nearby who are looking for action in your area. (You don't have to deal with registering for an account or anything — pull up the site, choose to browse anonymously, complete the age verification and captcha, and you're in.) The "Cruiser Filters" let you search for exactly what you're into, from body type to endowment size to your favorite sex positions.

As of April 2026, Sniffies is doubling down on speed with a few new updates. They just dropped "Cruiser Cards," a scrollable carousel that highlights active guys nearby so you don’t have to hunt around the map. They’ve also added a new "Into Filter" and "Position Icons" that put a cruiser’s intent and favorite sex positions directly on their map avatar.

When you're ready to meet, you can use the new "Share a Spot" feature to drop a temporary, expiring map pin directly into the chat. It’s much better than sending vague directions or swapping apps to share your location. They even added "Share a Group," which lets you send live group event details — like the time and who’s attending.

The app now has around three million monthly active users who send 20 million messages daily, and has even caught Match Group's attention. The company just invested $100 million in Sniffies, a deal that also gives Match an option to buy the platform outright.

If your idea of a perfect match is someone who can discuss the nuances of rope suspension one minute and step in as Dungeon Master for your next D&D night the next, you should probably be on FetLife. To be clear, FetLife is a social network for the kink community, not a hookup app in the typical sense. That means users might not appreciate it if you treat it like a swiping or swinging app. Still, as the online destination for established kinksters, it's a great place to meet new sexy friends who share your very specific interests.

We also think FetLife is a great place if you're looking for the best hookup app for gamers, for lack of a better option. While there isn't a hookup app made exclusively for gamers (at least, not one worth recommending), FetLife's user base includes a lot of self-described nerds, and there's a surprising amount of overlap between the gaming and kink communities.

Unlike swipe-based apps, FetLife operates as a social network. Weiss also recommends FetLife as a great destination for those with nerdy interests: "FetLife is popular among gamers and even has some subgroups specifically for kinky gamers," says Weiss. "The app/site tends to attract nerds and other fringe communities."

OkCupid (removed October 2026): OkCupid is still a solid pick for inclusive, values-driven dating, but it's a relationship app at heart. Feeld, HUD, and HER all do inclusivity better for no-strings fun. And after OkCupid's 2026 FTC settlement over sharing nearly 3 million users' photos with a facial recognition company, I'm not comfortable recommending it for something as private as hookups.

Hily (added August 2026): I’ve added Hily to our top picks because its free tier is surprisingly generous (up to 100 likes a day!) and its AI safety tech (like Consent Guard) makes it a standout option for casual, blunt daters looking for a fresh alternative to the Big Three.

Hinge (moved up October 2025): Hinge just keeps getting better, so I’ve bumped it up higher on my list. It still earns its spot for casual dating with personality; its user base is growing, and my recent tests have been surprisingly positive.

You might notice a few apps that pop up in ads or other lists are missing here. That’s intentional. I swipe through the good, the bad, and the downright sketchy so you don’t have to. For an app to make my list, it has to be effective, safe, and worth your time.

Here's a shortlist of apps that didn't make the cut:

Plenty of Fish: POF's rebrand didn't do it any favors. My last round of testing showed it removed key features like free messaging with non-matches, and I kept running into the same old profiles. (Removed January 2025.)

Match: Some people swear they've found casual hookups on Match, but that's not what it's for. It's still one of my top picks for a long-term relationship. For a hookup? You're fishing in the wrong pond. (Removed August 2025.)

Wild: You’ve probably seen ads for this one. On paper, Wild sounds like the perfect casual dating app. In practice, the paywalls are aggressive, the distance filter doesn't work, and you have to pay for anything that's even remotely useful. Unless you're willing to spend serious cash upfront (and hope for the best), the experience feels more limited than with more generous free options like Tinder or Hily.

DOWN: This app (formerly "Bang With Friends") is known for its simple "Get Down" vs. "Get Date" feature. It sounds clever, but in reality, the experience is messy at best. Many users report feeling scammed by subscriptions that don't deliver matches, or finding that the few real people on there are... let's say "odd." It’s hard to recommend an app when the main user complaint is "Is anyone real?" Hard pass.

Facebook Dating: Yes, Facebook has a dating section, and it’s surprisingly massive (and completely free, which is huge). While it's a decent option for casual dating, the vibe tends to be a bit more "friends of friends" and "relationship-focused" than the anonymous, no-strings energy you get from apps like Pure or Feeld. (For Mashable's Chance Townsend, signing up was "the most uneventful dating experience" of his life.) It's also added an AI dating assistant and "Meet Cute," which sends you one surprise match a week. It's worth a shot if you're already on Facebook, but it didn't quite crack my top tier for no-strings-attached hookups specifically.

Tinder is the best hookup app for most people because nearly everyone is on it, which means more chances to find someone looking for the same thing. For total anonymity, try Pure. For kink or ethical non-monogamy, go with Feeld. Queer men should start with Grindr or Sniffies, and queer women should try HER.

Yes. Tinder is trying to shake its hookup reputation with features like Events, Modes, and its brand-new Group Hangouts, but it's still the fastest way to find a casual connection. If anything, those IRL features make it even easier to meet someone in person, fast.

Tinder, Hinge, and Hily are the best free options. Tinder has the biggest free user pool, Hinge lets free users see who liked them, and Hily's free tier gives you up to 100 "likes" a day. Some apps, like Grindr, have gotten much more limited without a subscription.

Pure is the best anonymous hookup app. It never asks for your name, and chats and photos self-destruct after 24 hours. Just remember that anonymous doesn't mean you shouldn't be cautious: "Anonymous should never mean untraceable to YOU," says Arrechea. Use Pure's True Photo request to confirm you're talking to a real person before you meet.

Bumble is the best hookup app for women who want control over who reaches out. Only one opening message is allowed, and the chat stays locked until you reply. Pure is also free for women and lets you auto-block unsolicited nudes, and HER is our top pick for queer women.

Feeld is the best app for couples looking for a third. Its free Constellation feature lets you link your profile with up to five partners, so everyone's on the same page. "I often recommend this app to couples who want to find a third person to play with or date," says Weiss.

Yes, as long as you stick to apps with built-in protections and practice common sense when meeting strangers. When choosing which dating apps to use, look for features such as:

Photo or face verification: Tinder's Face Check requires new members to take a video selfie.

Nude filters: Pure's My Media Rules and Hily's Consent Guard block or warn you about explicit photos.

Location sharing: Pure's Safety Signal shares your live location with a trusted friend.

Blocking and reporting: Never use an app that makes it hard to report bad behavior.

Always meet in a public place first, get yourself there and home, and tell a friend where you'll be. "Casual sex does not require casual safety," says Sandra Hatton, professional matchmaker and founder of When We First. "Do not give a stranger your home address simply because the intention of the connection is casual." Weiss also recommends having a friend check in with you later that night or the next morning.

They pressure you to drink or host immediately.

They try to move the chat to WhatsApp right away.

Be honest and specific about what you want, like "Looking for a regular FWB" or your specific kinks if you're on Feeld. You don't need to spell out every detail. "The bio is there to open the right door, not to function as a legal contract," says Pappel.

Yes, Hinge works great for casual dating if you use the "Dating Intentions" section. Put "Short-Term" or "Figuring it out" on your profile so everyone knows why you're there. The profile prompts also help you gauge someone's personality before you meet up.

Go with Tinder if you want volume, since it has the biggest user base by far. Go with Bumble if you want a slower, more controlled pace. Only one opening message is allowed, and the chat doesn't unlock until the other person replies (they have 72 hours).

Yes, Scruff and Sniffies are great alternatives. Grindr still has the most guys online, but Scruff is the best pick for a more rugged, conversational crowd, and Sniffies is the place for map-based cruising.

In some cases, such as if you live in a small town or don't have time to wait for matches. In our Grindr review, we noted that Grindr Xtra can be worthwhile when you're traveling or during big events. However, you can typically make connections on apps like Tinder or Grindr using only the free versions.

Most hookup apps are free to download but lock key features, like seeing who liked you, behind a paywall. Hily and Tinder let you match and chat for free, while apps like Grindr and Feeld save their best features for paying members.

Recommending the best hookup apps isn't something I take lightly. Your time and, more importantly, your safety matter to me. That's why my selection process involves much more than blindly swiping left and right to see who is online.

If you're wondering how we choose the top platforms for casual dating, here’s exactly how I make sure my recommendations are trustworthy and genuinely helpful:

Hands-on testing: I personally create profiles and test out every single platform on this list, whether it's a mainstream app or a mobile hookup site like Sniffies. I look at how matching algorithms work in the real world and prioritize platforms that are intuitive, effective, and offer robust safety features (such as photo verification and reporting tools to prevent catfishing). If an app feels clunky, pushes too many annoying ads, or just gives off a bad vibe, it doesn't make the cut.

Expert and community feedback: I cross-reference my first-hand findings with real user reviews (yes, including Reddit threads) and consult with top relationship experts to ensure my picks are comprehensive. For this guide, I gathered insights from:

Suzannah Weiss, sex/couples therapist and resident sexologist for Erojoy

Sandra Hatton, professional matchmaker and founder of When We First

Erica Arrechea, founder and CEO of Cinqe Matchmaking

Caroline Millet, dating burnout coach and former matchmaker

Paulita Pappel, intimacy expert and founder of Lustery

Alexander Liebisch, CEO and founder of TinderProfile.ai

Michelle Herzog, LMFT, and AASECT-certified sex therapist

Continuous monitoring: The casual dating app world changes fast. My work doesn't stop after I hit publish. I continuously monitor app performance and feature updates, which means I'm ready to make tough calls and update my recommendations anytime an app no longer lives up to its promise.

Tabitha Britt is an award-winning freelance journalist, editor, and SEO/AEO strategist. Aside from reviewing dating apps and sex toys for Mashable, Tabitha is also the founding editor-in-chief of DO YOU ENDO — a digital magazine by individuals with endometriosis, for individuals with endometriosis. She has a Master's degree in Creative Publishing and Critical Journalism from The New School for Social Research and is a grad of Sextech School. You can find more of her work in various online publications, including National Geographic, Glamour, Better Homes & Gardens, and Everyday Health.

#320. Emma Heming Willis shares family photos as daughter Mabel turns 11

Bruce Willis’ wife, Emma Heming Willis, has celebrated their elder daughter’s birthday with a trip down memory lane.

Mabel Willis turned 11 on Sunday, and her proud mom marked the occasion by sharing a montage of family photos and videos taken over the years, set to the song “Pictures Of You” by The Cure.

“Happy 11th Birthday Mabel Ray!” Heming Willis wrote in the caption.

Emma Heming Willis speaks out about finding community as a caregiver: 'This journey can feel very dark'

“Your energy is infectious,” she continued, praising her little girl for the way she “can light a whole room with your smile and warmth.”

“How you love and care for your family and friends is beautiful to witness. Keep shining my love and always remember to #liveitup,” Heming Willis added.

Heming Willis and Willis married in 2009. Along with Mabel, the couple also have an 8-year-old daughter, Evelyn. Willis also has daughters Rumer, Scout and Tallulah with his ex-wife, Demi Moore.

Willis is clearly a doting dad. One picture in Heming Willis’ montage shows the “Die Hard” star holding baby Mabel while planting a kiss on her forehead, while a more recent image shows a beaming Willis hanging out in nature with his preteen.

Bruce Willis sings with his family in birthday tribute video from ex Demi Moore

Heming Willis penned an equally heartfelt tribute last month when her husband celebrated his 68th birthday. Sharing a video montage on Instagram, she referred to the actor as “pure love.”

In February, Willis’ family announced that his speaking disorder, aphasia, had progressed into a form of dementia called frontotemporal dementia, or FTD.

“Today there are no treatments for the disease, a reality that we hope can change in the years ahead,” they said in an update shared online. “As Bruce’s condition advances, we hope that any media attention can be focused on shining a light on this disease that needs far more awareness and research.”

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, FTD refers to “a group of disorders caused by progressive nerve cell loss in the brain’s frontal lobes (the areas behind your forehead) or its temporal lobes.” These areas of the brain are generally associated with personality, behavior and language.

#319. Whats new to streaming this week? (Nov. 6, 2026)

Don't be overwhelmed or waste an hour scrolling through your services to determine what to watch. We've got your back, whatever your mood. Mashable offers watch guides for all of the above, broken down by genre: comedy, thriller, horror, documentary, and animation, among others. But if you're seeking something brand new (or just new to streaming), we've got you covered there, too.

In 2005, the missing persons case of Natalee Holloway became national news when the 18-year-old from Tennessee vanished in Aruba. She was last seen with Dutchman Joran van der Sloot, who was an early person of interest and over the years has told conflicting stories of what came next.

Netflix's newest true crime doc series reexamines the case, offering interviews with authorities and Holloway's mother and friends, as well as previously unreleased footage. Directors Dani Sloane and Matthew Galkin teamed with Story Syndicate (Maternal Instinct, Titan: The Oceangate Disaster) for this three-part documentary series about a mother's quest to getting justice for her daughter. — Kristy Puchko, Entertainment Editor

How to watch: Taken: Natalee Holloway is now streaming on Netflix.

Look, I love a Netflix Christmas movie, but to be honest, this one looks outstandingly average. And I love dog movies. If you saw the 2017 Dennis Quaid-fronted drama A Dog’s Purpose or its sequel, 2019's A Dog's Journey, this is pretty much the same deal but set at Christmas. And that makes sense since all three movies (as well as A Dog's Way Home) are based on novels by W. Bruce Cameron, who has screenwriting credits on each movie. The rumply basset hound and pristine corgi puppy who are seemingly tasked with bringing a family together in yuletide unity are cute, but the trailer is not. — Shannon Connellan, Senior Editor

Starring: Dennis Quaid, Milo Ventimiglia, Brooke Lena Johnson, Thomas Haden Church, Mary Steenburgen, Kathleen Rose Perkins, Jennifer Tilly, Ethan Loomis, and Marissa Jaret Winokur

How to watch: A Dog's Perfect Christmas is now streaming on Netflix.

Psychic children abducted by the government and held in a brutal secure facility? It's a classic Stephen King formula, and The Institute — based on the horror author's novel of the same name — did well enough to bag itself a second outing. While the first season focused on new recruit Luke Ellis (Joe Freeman) surviving in his strange new prison, Season 2 looks set to widen its scope, with the main cast struggling to find evidence that'll expose the facility's corrupt practices. — Sam Haysom, General Assignment Editor, UK

Starring: Joe Freeman, Ben Barnes, Mary-Louise Parker, Alfie Allen, Simone Miller, Fionn Laird, Arlen So, Robert Joy, and Hannah Galway

How to watch: The Institute Season 2 premieres Nov. 8 at 9 p.m. ET on MGM+.

I'm sorry, but isn't The 12 Dates of Christmas already a movie? The cheeseball 2011 Groundhog Day scenario starring Amy Smart as a Scroogey woman stuck in a time loop of dates to teach her a lesson about being nicer to people? Well, this isn't that.

Hulu's identically named film reunites Pretty Little Liars stars Lucy Hale and Ian Harding in another romantic scenario, this time much less problematic than that show's student-teacher relationship. Will I be settling in to see Hale's character determined to thwart her own singlehood by going on 12 dates in 12 days at the busiest time of the year? As sure as a partridge in a pear tree. — S.C.

How to watch: The 12 Dates of Christmas premieres Nov. 6 on Hulu.

Vermont's finest return in Super Troopers 3, a madcap sequel from comedy troupe Broken Lizard. The film sees Farva (Kevin Heffernan) about to marry Thorny's (Jay Chandrasekhar) sister Sarita (Hannah Simone). Of course, all hell breaks loose thanks to a rowdy bachelor party and a new drug known as "Canadian Crystal." Can the troopers save this wedding (and make way for a new sequel in the process)? You'll have to stream to find out. — Belen Edwards, Entertainment Reporter

Starring: Jay Chandrasekhar, Kevin Heffernan, Steve Lemme, Paul Soter, Erik Stolhanske, Hannah Simone, Nat Faxon, Chace Crawford, Andrew Dismukes, Marisa Coughlan, Jon Rudnitsky, Lisa Gilroy, Sakina Jaffrey, Iqbal Theba, Lynda Carter, and Brian Cox

How to watch: Super Troopers 3 is now streaming on Hulu.

Almost anything can be scary in the right circumstances. That, at least, seems to be what writer/director Yûta Shimotsu is going for in New Group, a horror comedy largely centered around human pyramids. These start to pop at Ai's (Anna Yamada) new high school, and it soon becomes clear that the phenomenon is more disturbing than simple gymnastics. — S.H.

Starring: Anna Yamada, Yuzu Aoki, Arisa Sasaki, and Pierre Taki

How to watch: New Group debuts on Shudder on Nov. 6.

Andrew Garfield says "no kings" in The Uprising, the latest from director Paul Greengrass (The Bourne Supremacy). The film tells the story of England's 1381 Peasants' Revolt, with Garfield playing a fictionalized farmer at the center of it all.

While The Uprising's tale of standing up to tyranny is timely, critics found the film's execution lacking. As Mashable Entertainment Editor Kristy Puchko wrote in her review, "Greengrass gives us a bland, muddy slog with a black-and-white hero and villain, and an ending that is sure to satisfy no one."* — B.E.

Starring: Andrew Garfield, Jamie Bell, Stephen Dillane, Tom Hollander, Cosmo Jarvis, Thomasin McKenzie, Jonny Lee Miller, Woody Norman, and Katherine Waterston

How to watch: The Uprising premieres Nov. 6 on Peacock.

Romantic drama Charlie Harper hits digital this week — and no, it is not about someone named Charlie Harper, but rather about the love story between Charlie (Nick Robinson) and Harper (Emilia Jones). The film uses a nonlinear approach to tell the story of this pair's relationship, from their sweetest moments to their most tumultuous. Critics didn't fall completely in love with Charlie Harper, but if you're looking for some onscreen romance, it's definitely worth a shot. — B.E.

How to watch: Charlie Harper is now available on digital.

Yes, there is a new Korean romantic epic streaming this week, and yes, it does come with a heap of buzz from this year's Busan International Film Festival. Based on the hugely popular Naver WEBTOON, The Remarried Empress sees a royal relationship in peril, that of the Eastern Empire's Empress Navier (Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha's Shin Min-a) and Emperor Sovieshu (Kingdom's Ju Ji-hoon). When the emperor's affections stray elsewhere, the empress makes one hell of a deal: She wants to remarry. And not just anyone; she's got her eye on Heinrey, the rival Western Kingdom's dreamy crown prince (Law and the City's Lee Jong-suk). The very future of the kingdoms are at stake! — S.C.

Starring: Shin Min-a, Ju Ji-hoon, Lee Jong-suk, and Lee Se-young

How to watch: The Remarried Empress is now streaming on Disney+ and Hulu.

If you're after a steampunk anime western from Yasuke creator LeSean Thomas, Netflix's Bass X Machina will fit your wanted poster. In the six-episode animated series, Oscar-nominated Causeway star Brian Tyree Henry voices Bass Reeves, a character based on the real American frontier icon who was one of the first Black U.S. Deputy Marshals west of the Mississippi. Expect a world of ruthless outlaws, desert machines, and otherworldly forces as one man tries to protect his family and deliver justice. — S.C.

Starring: Brian Tyree Henry, Janelle Monáe, Tati Gabrielle, Cree Summer, Chaske Spencer, Currie Graham, and Starletta DuPois

How to watch: Bass X Machina is now streaming on Netflix.

Owen Wilson's sports comedy Stick made a sweet splash in its first season, telling a story of golf redemption and found family. Now, Wilson returns as ex-golfer Pryce Cahill, who's coaching 17-year-old golf prodigy Santi Wheeler (Peter Dager). As Santi continues his pro golfing career, Pryce makes the game-changing decision to mount a comeback and try to become the oldest golfer to win a major championship. To accomplish that feat, he'll need some help, and Apple has recruited Pluribus Emmy winner Rhea Seehorn for the job. She plays Coach Amanda, a "swing doctor" who might just take Pryce back to his glory days. — B.E.

Starring: Owen Wilson, Peter Dager, Marc Maron, Mariana Treviño, Lilli Kay, Judy Greer, Timothy Olyphant, Rhea Seehorn, John Higgins, Billy Zane, Rex Linn, Sasha Alexander, and Missi Pyle

How to watch: The first two episodes of Stick Season 2 are now streaming on AppleTV, with new episodes every Wednesday.

Thirty years after Marian Keyes' first Walsh sisters book was published, the BBC finally brought the lives of Rachel, Anna, Claire, Maggie, and Helen Walsh to UK screens in February. Now, The Walsh Sisters is streaming in the U.S. through Roku. From Stefanie Preissner (Can't Cope, Won't Cope) and Kefi Chadwick (Rivals) comes a deeply moving adaptation that weaves several Keyes' books together — and boasts an incredible cast. As I wrote in my review, "A raw, authentic portrayal of sisterhood, addiction, grief, and mental health, The Walsh Sisters feels well overdue on our screens." — S.C.

Starring: Caroline Menton, Danielle Galligan, Stefanie Preissner, Máiread Tyers, and Louisa Harland

How to watch: The Walsh Sisters is now streaming on Roku.

An ancient serpentine predator lies in slumber, deep in the Amazon, in this Anaconda-style creature survival horror from director Mike P. Nelson (V/H/S/85; Silent Night, Deadly Night).

Beware Boiúna sees a group on a medical mission into the South American rainforest hunted by a mythical semiaquatic reptile who's recently been rudely awakened. Kiana Madeira (Fear Street), Jessica Rothe (Happy Death Day), and Logan Marshall-Green (Upgrade) disturb the slumber of Boiúna, whose bite is way worse than her non-existent bark. Written by Nelson with his Wrong Turn collaborator Alan B. McElroy and Doom: Annihilation's Tony Giglio, this film feels meant to be bravely watched in cinemas behind an enormous popcorn bucket — but now you can watch it from the comfort of your sofa.* — S.C.

Starring: Kiana Madeira, Jessica Rothe, and Logan Marshall-Green

How to watch: Beware Boiúna is now available on digital.

Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw return for spy shenanigans in Season 2 of Black Doves, and the stakes (and suspense) have never been higher.

Helen (Knightley) is still giving up England's secrets to the Black Doves, even as her husband, Wallace (Andrew Buchan), gets ready to take on the role of Prime Minister. Meanwhile, triggerman Sam (Whishaw) is stuck taking smaller hit jobs. However, the two reunite when a sinister plot to undermine Reed's (Sarah Lancashire) position in the Black Doves emerges. It's not long before the two are sucked back into a web of espionage, violence, and most importantly of all, friendship.* — B.E.

Starring: Keira Knightley, Ben Whishaw, Sarah Lancashire, Andrew Buchan, Kathryn Hunter, Ella Lily Hyland, Gabrielle Creevy, Agnes O’Casey, and Molly Chesworth

How to watch: Black Doves Season 2 is now streaming on Netflix.

Director Georgia Oakley (Blue Jean) and screenwriter Diana Reid adapt Jane Austen's 1811 novel about two very different sisters seeking a match in Regency-era England.

After the death of their father, the rigorously rational Elinor Dashwood (Daisy Edgar-Jones) and her impulsive younger sister Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles) are eager to find husbands. But they're looking for something more rare than financial security. They're looking for love in a world of infuriatingly righteous gentlemen and unfortunately sexy rogues.* — K.P.

Starring: Daisy Edgar-Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe, Bodhi Rae Breathnach, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, and Fiona Shaw

How to watch: Sense and Sensibility is now available for rental or purchase on digital.

Before Lance Oppenheim blew our minds with You Can See Everything, he dropped Primetime, a docudrama exploring Chris Hansen's problematic news special series To Catch a Predator.

Robert Pattinson is chilling and uncomfortably funny in the lead role of Hansen, reimagining the real-life newsman as a creepy clown with a dangerous blind ambition. And while Oppenheim and a talented cast make a movie that is thought-provoking, this critic hoped it'd go harder. As I wrote in my review, "I was left wishing Primetime had the guts to follow the dark path this heightened Hansen charted to somewhere deranged, perhaps providing a more satisfying ending than real life (and reality TV) has. Chase those midnight movie vibes that Pattinson has coursing through his final act into something damning and daring! Or, don't, I guess.

"While Primetime is exhilarating and disturbing thanks to its sensational cast, a flimsy conclusion has this film end with a whimper instead of a bang." — K.P.

Starring: Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo, and Phoebe Bridgers

How to watch: Primetime is now available on digital.

Director John Wilson, of HBO's How To with John Wilson, makes his feature directorial debut with documentary The History of Concrete. Don't be fooled by the seemingly dry title. The History of Concrete is an absurd deep dive into the gray material that surrounds us, one that involves everything from Hallmark movies to gum-busting machines. If you enjoyed How To with John Wilson or want another meta-documentary after seeing You Can See Everything, this should scratch that itch. — B.E.

How to watch: The History of Concrete is now available on digital.

Alex Gibney's Musk documentary had a blink-and-you'll-miss-it theatrical run, being pulled from cinemas after just two weeks. But if you didn't get chance to see the nearly four-hour doc — which charts the rise to power of the world's richest man, featuring interviews with family members and former colleagues — you can catch it on digital this week. Mashable's Matt Binder described it as "brutal and accurate" in his review for Mashable. It struggled at the box office, but had its marketing campaign hampered due to ads being restricted on multiple social networks. — S.H.

How to watch: Musk is now available on digital.

Jess McKenna and Zach Reino have made their mark on Dropout with improvised musical numbers on Play It By Ear and Game Changer, including the finale "Last Talent Standing." Now, they're bringing their song-writing skills to the comedy streamer's first scripted series in seven years, MP3.

Seemingly inspired by the TRL days of MTV, MP3 focuses on a TV show where host Dane Cartel (Jeremy Culhane) offers up music videos alongside his new co-hosts Chia (Aparna Nancherla) and Dr. Muse-Tina (Skye Townsend). This setup allows Dropout's wide ensemble of comedians to pop up for kooky cameos, singing and dancing in a variety of bizarre music videos. Plus, based on the trailer, this show shares a universe with Very Important People. So, watch out for the epic return of Princess Emily. — K.P.

Starring: Jeremy Culhane, Paul F. Tompkins, Zach Reino, Aparna Nancherla, Skye Townsend, and Jess McKenna

How to watch: MP3 is now streaming on Dropout.

Teachers deserve better. Our underpaid educators put up with everything from disruptive students to micromanaging parents. And in Jonatan Etzler's dark comedy thriller Bad Apples, one (Saoirse Ronan) takes matters into her own hands. Written by Jess O'Kane as an adaptation of Rasmus Andersson's novel De Oönskade, the film sees Ronan as Somerset-based primary school teacher Maria. She loves teaching, despite the underfunded education system testing her daily. When troubled student Danny (newcomer Eddie Waller) constantly disrupts her class, Maria makes some choices.

As I wrote in my review, "With Ronan's always-impeccable talents supported by a sublime young cast, Bad Apples leans into unethical impulses, all the while exposing home truths about the under-resourced education system and social disdain toward children with behavioural, emotional, and social difficulties. Plus, it's really funny."* — S.C.

Starring: Saoirse Ronan, Eddie Waller, Jacob Anderson, Rakie Ayola, Robert Emms, Sean Gilder, and Kerry Howard

How to watch: Bad Apples is now available on digital.

One of 2025's best TV surprises was Canadian comedy North of North, a small town sitcom set in the Arctic Circle. Young Inuk mother Siaja (Anna Lambe) decides to blow up her unhappy marriage and start fresh, embarking on a warm, moving journey of self-discovery. That journey continues in Season 2, which will see Siaja try to keep leveling up her life, professionally and personally, even if it means making some big mistakes in the process. Wherever your new road takes you, Siaja, we can't wait to keep supporting you!* — B.E.

Starring: Anna Lambe, Maika Harper, Braeden Clarke, Jay Ryan, Mary Lynn Rajskub, Zorga Qaunaq, Bailey Poching, Nutaaq Doreen Simmonds, Keira Belle Cooper, and Bruce McCulloch

How to watch: North of North Season 2 is now streaming on Netflix.

If you're on the hunt for surgically precise joke writing and an impeccable ensemble, I've got one name for you: Reggie. Dinkins.

Created by 30 Rock's Robert Carlock and Sam Means, The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins cemented itself as one of the year's best comedies when it premiered this January. Now, it's back and bound to deliver more riotous one-liners and pop culture references. The series follows disgraced New York Jets star Reggie Dinkins (Tracy Morgan) and documentarian Arthur Tobin (Daniel Radcliffe), who's making a film about Reggie's life. Morgan and Radcliffe are a duo to die for, and Erika Alexander and Bobby Moynihan are riots in their supporting roles. Buy into the ridiculousness and have the best time.* — B.E.

Starring: Tracy Morgan, Daniel Radcliffe, Erika Alexander, Bobby Moynihan, Precious Way, and Jalyn Hall

How to watch: The first episode of The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins Season 2 is now streaming on Peacock. New episodes premiere Mondays at 8:30 p.m. ET on NBC, with episodes available on Peacock the next day.

Good news, everyone! You can watch Weapons director Zach Cregger's Resident Evil reboot at home this week. The adaptation of Capcom's popular horror game franchise was co-written by Cregger with John Wick: Chapter 4's Shay Hatten, with horror and action through the roof. Except this time the Resident Evil chaos is happening to a regular Raccoon City resident (Austin Abrams) who just can't seem to figure out those damn locks. — S.C.

Starring: Austin Abrams, Zach Cherry, Kali Reis, and Paul Walter Hauser

How to watch: Resident Evil is now available on digital.

Leo Reich's new comedy It Gets Worse set the internet ablaze when Channel 4 released an NSFW clip involving Andrew Scott as a therapist. And while that's certainly a great hook, especially for everyone who's still not over Scott's role in Fleabag, it's far from the best thing about this beautifully messy series.

Reich stars as 24-year-old Ethan, who's going through the catastrophic double whammy of a quarter life crisis and eviction from the London apartment he shares with his two best friends from university, Abi (Emily Fairn) and Sam (Olive Gray). As the three try to find a new place, they split up across the city, where they each face a harrowing question familiar to anyone in their early 20s: What the hell am I going to do with my life? To find answers (if there are any), Reich spins a tale of fraught friendships, awkward hookups, and hard truths sure to make any young 20-something at a crossroads feel seen. — B.E.

Starring: Leo Reich, Emily Fairn, Olive Gray, Sean Delaney, Dane Williams, India Mullen, John Tothill, Andrew Scott, Lena Dunham, and Amelia Dimoldenberg

How to watch: All episodes of It Gets Worse premiere Nov. 6 on Paramount+.
